# yaml-language-server: $schema=../../schema/question.schema.json

locales:
  ru:
    title: Какую политику команды вы зададите для сторонних JavaScript-библиотек в компонентах Blazor?
    prompt: |
      В приложении Blazor Web App на .NET 10 используются режимы `InteractiveServer` и `InteractiveWebAssembly`.
      Разные команды подключают сторонние JavaScript-библиотеки (графики, редактор текста, карты): добавляют теги
      `<script>` в разметку, объявляют функции в `window` и вызывают их из компонентов через
      `JS.InvokeVoidAsync("chartLib.render", ...)`. В production уже были ошибки при пререндеринге, утечки памяти
      на сервере и поломка после обновления одной из библиотек.

      Какие правила работы со сторонними JS-библиотеками вы введёте для команды и как будете их поддерживать?
    hint: |
      Что происходит, когда двадцать компонентов обращаются к одной библиотеке по строковому имени: что проверит
      компилятор, что случится при пререндеринге и кто освободит ресурсы после навигации?
    answer: |
      1. **Одна обёртка на библиотеку.** Компоненты не вызывают функции библиотеки по строковым именам. У каждой
         библиотеки есть владелец и один типизированный C#-слой: компонент, если библиотека управляет DOM-элементом
         (график, редактор), или сервис за интерфейсом, если API невизуальный (буфер обмена, геолокация).
         Наружу выходят только C#-типы, а строковые идентификаторы и форма JSON живут в одном месте.
      2. **Изолированный ES-модуль вместо глобальных функций.** Обёртка поставляет небольшой JS-модуль (рядом с
         компонентом в файле `.razor.js` или в `wwwroot` библиотеки Razor-классов), который импортирует библиотеку
         и экспортирует несколько функций. C#-сторона загружает его лениво через
         `InvokeAsync<IJSObjectReference>("import", path)`. Никаких функций в `window` и тегов `<script>` на страницах.
      3. **Явный жизненный цикл.** Обёртка реализует `IAsyncDisposable`: вызывает у экземпляра библиотеки её
         функцию уничтожения, освобождает `IJSObjectReference` модуля и экземпляров и каждую созданную
         `DotNetObjectReference`. В `DisposeAsync` перехватывается `JSDisconnectedException`, потому что в серверном
         режиме соединение с браузером к этому моменту может уже исчезнуть.
      4. **Работа в любом режиме отрисовки.** Первый вызов только в `OnAfterRenderAsync` при `firstRender`, потому
         что при пререндеринге и статической отрисовке на сервере браузера ещё нет. Только асинхронные вызовы:
         `IJSInProcessRuntime` есть лишь в WebAssembly. Маленькие сообщения без частых вызовов в циклах, большие
         данные через потоки. `[JSImport]` и `[JSExport]` допустимы только в коде, который работает исключительно в
         WebAssembly.
      5. **Границы DOM.** Библиотека получает через `ElementReference` пустой элемент, внутрь которого Blazor ничего
         не отрисовывает. Blazor не должен рендерить в DOM, который меняет библиотека.
      6. **Допуск и поставка.** Новая библиотека проходит ревью: лицензия, размер, активность сопровождения, нет ли
         готового Blazor-компонента. Версия закреплена, файлы отдаются приложением (или с CDN с SRI), совместимость с
         CSP проверена. Обновление библиотеки затрагивает только её обёртку.
      7. **Тесты и контроль.** Компоненты тестируются с подменённым интерфейсом обёртки. Правило в code review и, по
         возможности, анализатор запрещённых API: `IJSRuntime` внедряется только в каталоге обёрток.
    explanation: |
      Разрозненные строковые вызовы переносят все ошибки во время выполнения: переименование функции, другой порядок
      аргументов или новая мажорная версия библиотеки компилятор не заметит. Каждое место вызова заново повторяет
      одни и те же ошибки: обращение к JS в `OnInitializedAsync` при пререндеринге, забытое освобождение ресурсов,
      синхронный вызов, который работает в WebAssembly и не работает на сервере. Обёртка решает эти задачи один раз
      и делает их проверяемыми.

      Освобождение ресурсов критично именно в серверном режиме. `DotNetObjectReference` удерживает .NET-объект от
      сборщика мусора, пока ссылку не освободят, а `IJSObjectReference` удерживает объект на стороне JavaScript.
      Без `Dispose` они живут до конца circuit, и у приложения с долгими сессиями растёт память на сервере и в
      браузере. Изолированные модули убирают конфликты глобальных имён и позволяют загружать библиотеку только там,
      где она нужна.

      Правило про DOM нужно потому, что Blazor сравнивает своё дерево отрисовки с DOM, которым, по его мнению, он
      управляет. Если библиотека меняет эти узлы, следующий diff даёт непредсказуемый результат.

      Политика - это не запрет на JavaScript, а процесс: у библиотеки есть владелец, точка входа и правила, которые
      проверяются ревью и тестами. Поведение режимов отрисовки описано для Blazor Web App начиная с .NET 8 и верно
      для .NET 10.
    linkTitles:
      - "Вызов функций JavaScript из методов .NET в Blazor"
      - "Взаимодействие с JavaScript в Blazor"
      - "Вызов методов .NET из функций JavaScript в Blazor"
  en:
    title: What policy do you set for third-party JavaScript libraries in Blazor components?
    prompt: |
      A Blazor Web App on .NET 10 uses the `InteractiveServer` and `InteractiveWebAssembly` render modes.
      Different teams plug in third-party JavaScript libraries (charts, a text editor, maps): they add `<script>`
      tags to the markup, declare functions on `window` and call them from components with
      `JS.InvokeVoidAsync("chartLib.render", ...)`. Production has already seen failures during prerendering, memory
      leaks on the server and breakage after one of the libraries was upgraded.

      Which rules for third-party JS libraries do you introduce for the team, and how do you keep them in place?
    hint: |
      What happens when twenty components call the same library by a string name: what does the compiler check,
      what happens during prerendering, and who releases the resources after navigation?
    answer: |
      1. **One wrapper per library.** Components do not call library functions by string names. Every library has
         an owner and one typed C# layer: a component if the library manages a DOM element (a chart, an editor), or
         a service behind an interface if the API is non-visual (clipboard, geolocation). Only C# types are exposed,
         and string identifiers and the JSON shape live in one place.
      2. **An isolated ES module instead of globals.** The wrapper ships a small JS module (collocated in a
         `.razor.js` file or in `wwwroot` of a Razor class library) that imports the library and exports a few
         functions. The C# side loads it lazily with `InvokeAsync<IJSObjectReference>("import", path)`. No functions
         on `window` and no `<script>` tags on pages.
      3. **An explicit lifetime.** The wrapper implements `IAsyncDisposable`: it calls the library's destroy function
         for its instance, disposes the `IJSObjectReference` of the module and of the instances, and every
         `DotNetObjectReference` it created. `DisposeAsync` catches `JSDisconnectedException`, because in server mode
         the connection to the browser may already be gone at that point.
      4. **Works in every render mode.** The first call happens only in `OnAfterRenderAsync` when `firstRender` is
         true, because during prerendering and static server rendering there is no browser yet. Only asynchronous
         calls: `IJSInProcessRuntime` exists only in WebAssembly. Small messages and no chatty calls in loops; large
         data goes through streams. `[JSImport]` and `[JSExport]` are allowed only in code that runs exclusively in
         WebAssembly.
      5. **DOM boundaries.** The library receives, through an `ElementReference`, an empty element into which Blazor
         renders nothing. Blazor must not render into DOM that the library changes.
      6. **Admission and delivery.** A new library goes through review: licence, size, maintenance activity, whether
         a ready Blazor component exists. The version is pinned, the files are served by the app (or from a CDN with
         SRI), and CSP compatibility is checked. Upgrading a library touches only its wrapper.
      7. **Tests and enforcement.** Components are tested with a substituted wrapper interface. A code review rule
         and, where possible, a banned API analyzer: `IJSRuntime` is injected only in the wrappers folder.
    explanation: |
      Scattered string-named calls move every error to run time: a renamed function, a different argument order or
      a new major version of the library is invisible to the compiler. Every call site repeats the same mistakes on
      its own: JS interop in `OnInitializedAsync` during prerendering, forgotten cleanup, a synchronous call that
      works in WebAssembly and fails on the server. A wrapper solves these problems once and makes them testable.

      Cleanup matters most in server mode. A `DotNetObjectReference` keeps the .NET object from the garbage
      collector until the reference is disposed, and an `IJSObjectReference` keeps the object alive on the
      JavaScript side. Without disposal they live until the circuit ends, and an app with long sessions grows memory
      on both the server and the browser. Isolated modules remove global name clashes and let the library load only
      where it is needed.

      The DOM rule exists because Blazor compares its render tree with the DOM it believes it manages. If a library
      changes those nodes, the next diff gives unpredictable results.

      The policy is not a ban on JavaScript but a process: each library has an owner, an entry point and rules that
      review and tests enforce. The render mode behaviour is described for Blazor Web Apps since .NET 8 and holds
      for .NET 10.
    linkTitles:
      - "Call JavaScript functions from .NET methods in ASP.NET Core Blazor"
      - "ASP.NET Core Blazor JavaScript interoperability"
      - "Call .NET methods from JavaScript functions in ASP.NET Core Blazor"

# yaml-language-server: $schema=../../schema/question.schema.json

locales:
  ru:
    title: Правила валидации в формах Blazor WebAssembly и в API разошлись, и в базу попали плохие данные. Что вы измените?
    prompt: |
      Команда поддерживает приложение Blazor WebAssembly на .NET 10 и ASP.NET Core API, в который оно пишет данные.
      Формы построены на `EditForm` с `DataAnnotationsValidator`, атрибуты валидации стоят на клиентских моделях.
      У API свои DTO и проверки, написанные вручную. За год правила разошлись: форма ограничивает скидку диапазоном
      0-30% и проверяет формат email, а API проверяет только обязательность полей.

      В базе нашлись заказы со скидкой 90% и некорректными email. Часть из них пришла от интеграционного скрипта,
      который вызывает API напрямую, часть - от пользователей с закэшированной старой версией клиента.

      Вы технический лидер. Что вы измените в коде, в данных и в процессе команды?
    hint: |
      Где на самом деле выполняется код клиентской валидации и кто, кроме вашей формы, может отправить запрос
      в API? Сколько копий одного правила должно существовать?
    answer: |
      1. **Закрыть дыру на сервере сразу.** API - единственная граница доверия: каждый пишущий эндпоинт проверяет
         запрос сам, даже если временно придётся продублировать правила. Для ключевых инвариантов добавить
         ограничения в базе (`CHECK` на диапазон скидки, `NOT NULL`, длины столбцов) как последний рубеж.
      2. **Разобраться с уже попавшими данными.** Найти некорректные строки запросом, по логам определить
         источники (скрипт, старый клиент), вместе с владельцем бизнеса решить, что исправить, а что пометить,
         и выполнить исправление отдельной миграцией данных до включения ограничений в базе.
      3. **Оставить одну копию правил.** Вынести DTO запросов с атрибутами валидации в общую библиотеку классов,
         на которую ссылаются и клиент, и API. Форма использует этот DTO как модель `EditForm`, а API проверяет
         тот же тип: контроллер с `[ApiController]` автоматически отвечает 400 с `ValidationProblemDetails`.
         Если команда предпочитает отдельные классы-валидаторы, они тоже живут в общей библиотеке.
      4. **Помнить, что библиотека уходит в браузер.** В ней только модели и правила: никаких секретов,
         строк подключения, EF Core и других серверных зависимостей. Правила, которым нужны данные (уникальность,
         остатки, права доступа), остаются только на сервере.
      5. **Показывать ошибки сервера в форме.** Ответ 400 разбирать и выводить ошибки у полей через
         `ValidationMessageStore` (компонент-валидатор, как в документации Blazor), чтобы серверные правила
         не выглядели для пользователя как «что-то сломалось».
      6. **Закрепить процессом.** Правило меняется только в общей библиотеке; на него есть табличные тесты
         валидных и невалидных значений; интеграционные тесты API отправляют невалидные запросы и ждут 400;
         в code review довод «клиент уже проверил» не принимается.
      7. **Учесть расхождение версий.** Старый клиент из кэша браузера будет присылать запросы по старым правилам.
         API отвечает ему понятными ошибками валидации, а не 500, и строгие правила включаются после миграции
         данных и предупреждения владельцев интеграций.
    explanation: |
      Клиентская валидация в Blazor WebAssembly - это удобство для пользователя, а не защита. Сборки приложения
      скачиваются в браузер и выполняются на машине пользователя: их можно изучить и изменить, а запрос в API
      можно отправить вообще без формы, как это делал интеграционный скрипт. Документация по безопасности Blazor
      прямо говорит, что проверкам на клиенте доверять нельзя и решения должен принимать сервер. Поэтому
      первое действие - серверная проверка, а не починка формы.

      Правила разошлись потому, что существовали в двух копиях, которые меняли разные люди. Общий C#-код для
      клиента и сервера - одно из главных преимуществ Blazor: один DTO с атрибутами даёт одинаковые проверки в
      `DataAnnotationsValidator` и в валидации модели ASP.NET Core. При этом общая библиотека не отменяет
      серверной проверки: она лишь гарантирует, что клиент и сервер проверяют одно и то же, а сервер всё равно
      проверяет всегда.

      Не всё можно разделить: правило «email уникален» требует базы, поэтому сервер должен уметь вернуть
      ошибку поля, а форма - показать её. Ограничения в базе ловят то, что прошло мимо кода (скрипты, ошибки
      в новых эндпоинтах), но дают плохие сообщения об ошибках, поэтому это страховка, а не основной механизм.
      Отдельный риск для лида - порядок выкатки: если включить ограничение в базе до очистки данных, миграция
      упадёт, а если ужесточить API без предупреждения, сломаются интеграции.

      Описание соответствует Blazor и ASP.NET Core в .NET 10.
    linkTitles:
      - "Валидация форм в ASP.NET Core Blazor"
      - "Безопасность и Identity в ASP.NET Core Blazor"
      - "Валидация модели в ASP.NET Core MVC и Razor Pages"
  en:
    title: Validation rules in Blazor WebAssembly forms and in the API have drifted apart and let bad data in. What do you change?
    prompt: |
      The team maintains a Blazor WebAssembly app on .NET 10 and the ASP.NET Core API it writes to.
      Forms are built with `EditForm` and `DataAnnotationsValidator`, and the validation attributes sit on client-side models.
      The API has its own DTOs and hand-written checks. Over a year the rules drifted apart: the form limits the discount
      to 0-30% and checks the email format, while the API checks only that fields are present.

      The database now contains orders with a 90% discount and invalid emails. Some came from an integration script
      that calls the API directly, some from users running an older cached version of the client.

      You are the tech lead. What do you change in the code, in the data and in the team's process?
    hint: |
      Where does the client-side validation code actually run, and who besides your form can send a request
      to the API? How many copies of one rule should exist?
    answer: |
      1. **Close the hole on the server first.** The API is the only trust boundary: every write endpoint validates
         the request itself, even if that means duplicating rules for a while. Add database constraints for the key
         invariants (a `CHECK` on the discount range, `NOT NULL`, column lengths) as the last line of defence.
      2. **Deal with the data that is already in.** Find the invalid rows with a query, use logs to identify the
         sources (the script, the old client), decide with the business owner what to fix and what to flag, and run
         the fix as a separate data migration before the database constraints are enabled.

         library referenced by both the client and the API. The form uses that DTO as the `EditForm` model, and the
         API validates the same type: a controller with `[ApiController]` automatically answers 400 with
         `ValidationProblemDetails`. If the team prefers separate validator classes, they live in the shared library too.

         strings, no EF Core or other server dependencies. Rules that need data (uniqueness, stock, permissions) stay
         on the server only.
      5. **Show server errors in the form.** Parse the 400 response and show the errors next to the fields with a
         `ValidationMessageStore` (a validator component, as in the Blazor docs), so server rules do not look to the
         user like "something broke".

         invalid values; API integration tests send invalid requests and expect 400; in code review "the client already
         checked it" is not accepted.
      7. **Plan for version skew.** An old client from the browser cache will keep sending requests under the old rules.
         The API answers it with clear validation errors, not 500, and strict rules are switched on after the data
         migration and after the owners of integrations are warned.
    explanation: |
      Client-side validation in Blazor WebAssembly is a convenience for the user, not protection. The app assemblies are
      downloaded to the browser and run on the user's machine: they can be inspected and modified, and a request can be
      sent to the API with no form at all, as the integration script did. The Blazor security docs state plainly that
      client-side checks cannot be trusted and that the server must make the decisions. That is why the first action is
      server validation, not fixing the form.

      The rules drifted because they existed in two copies changed by different people. Sharing C# code between client
      and server is one of the main advantages of Blazor: one DTO with attributes gives the same checks in
      `DataAnnotationsValidator` and in ASP.NET Core model validation. The shared library does not replace server
      validation, though: it only guarantees that client and server check the same thing, while the server always checks.

      Not everything can be shared: "the email is unique" needs the database, so the server must be able to return a
      field error and the form must be able to show it. Database constraints catch what got past the code (scripts, bugs
      in endpoints added later), but they produce poor error messages, so they are a safety net, not the main mechanism.
      A specific risk for a lead is the rollout order: enable a database constraint before cleaning the data and the
      migration fails; tighten the API without warning and integrations break.

      The description applies to Blazor and ASP.NET Core in .NET 10.

  en:
    title: "An InteractiveServer Blazor app built for one office must serve several continents: how do you redesign hosting and render modes?"
    prompt: |
      An internal Blazor Web App on .NET 10 was built for one office: global interactivity with the
      `InteractiveServer` render mode, one app server and a SQL Server database in the same region as the office.
      The company now opens the app to employees and partners on several continents.

      Distant users complain: typing in the search field lags, buttons react with a visible delay, and on mobile
      networks the reconnection overlay appears often. Management asks for one plan that makes the app usable
      worldwide.

      How do you redesign hosting and render modes, and in what order?
    hint: |
      What does one click cost in each render mode, and where does the state of an `InteractiveServer` user live?
    answer: |
      1. **Measure before redesigning.** Collect round-trip latency and reconnect counts per user region, find the
         chattiest interactions (`@bind:event="oninput"`, handlers of frequent events, large render diffs) and find
         out which pages actually need interactivity.
      2. **Stop making every page interactive on the server.** Replace global `InteractiveServer` with render modes
         per page and per component:
         - read-mostly pages (lists, reports, details) as static server-side rendering (static SSR) with streaming
           rendering and enhanced navigation: one request per navigation, no circuit, and responses can be cached
           close to users;
         - highly interactive screens for distant users (editors, grids, dashboards with filters) as
           `InteractiveWebAssembly` or `InteractiveAuto`: UI events are handled in the browser, and only data
           requests go over the network;
         - `InteractiveServer` stays only where users are close to the server or where code must not leave it.
      3. **Restructure the code for WebAssembly.** Components that used `DbContext` or server services directly
         depend on an interface: a server implementation and a client implementation over `HttpClient` that calls a
         web API. Secrets and authorization stay in the API, and the API checks every request, because WebAssembly
         code runs on the user's machine and can be read. Set a budget for the download size (trimming, lazy loading
         of assemblies) and check startup on weak devices.
      4. **Deploy per region.** Run the app and the API in several regions behind a global entry point (geo DNS
         routing or a global load balancer) that sends each user to the nearest region. The remaining
         `InteractiveServer` traffic needs WebSockets along the whole path and session affinity: a circuit lives in
         the memory of one server, so all its connections must reach that server in that region (sticky sessions,
         or Azure SignalR Service with the client bound to its server).
      5. **Bring the data along.** A nearby region helps little if every request still crosses the ocean to one
         database: add read replicas or caches per region, decide where writes go (a primary region, or
         partitioning by tenant or region) and check data residency requirements.
      6. **Plan for disconnects.** Keep durable state out of the circuit (database, URL, browser storage), tune the
         reconnect UI and the retention of disconnected circuits, roll out region by region and compare against the
         metrics from step 1.
    explanation: |
      In `InteractiveServer` the component lives on the server: every click, every key press with an `oninput`
      binding, every handler is a message to the server over SignalR and a render diff back. In one office the
      round trip takes milliseconds and nobody notices. Across continents it costs a noticeable fraction of a second
      per interaction, and any network glitch breaks the connection. A circuit cannot move to another server or
      region: the user either reconnects to the same server or loses the state. Scaling is expensive too: every
      connected user holds a circuit in server memory.

      Adding servers in the same region does not help: the bottleneck is distance and the network path, not CPU.
      So you either remove the round trip from the interaction (WebAssembly handles events locally, and static SSR
      has no interaction cost except navigation) or shorten it (a region near the user). Usually you need both:
      WebAssembly for interaction, regions for the first load, API calls and data.

      Every option has a price: WebAssembly means a download and startup in the browser, public code and a separate
      API layer; `InteractiveAuto` requires the component to work in both environments; static SSR gives up rich
      interactivity; several regions bring data replication and consistency questions. The architect's job is to
      pick a mode per product surface, not one mode for the whole app. Render modes in a Blazor Web App appeared in
      .NET 8, and this description holds for .NET 10.
    linkTitles:
      - "ASP.NET Core Blazor hosting models"
      - "Host and deploy ASP.NET Core server-side Blazor apps"
      - "ASP.NET Core Blazor render modes"

  en:
    title: "How do you choose between Blazor and a JavaScript SPA framework for a product that will live for many years?"
    prompt: |
      A company with a strong .NET team starts a product that must be developed and maintained for many years.
      The product has public pages, a customer account area with forms and grids, and an admin area. Some
      architects propose Blazor (a Blazor Web App on .NET 10), others propose an SPA on a JavaScript/TypeScript
      framework on top of an ASP.NET Core HTTP API.

      How do you make this decision: which criteria do you weigh, at what level do you decide, and how do you
      reduce the risk of being wrong for years ahead?
    hint: |
      Do different parts of the product have the same needs for first load, interactivity and SEO, and which
      properties of the team and the market change more slowly than frameworks do?
    answer: |
      1. **Decide per product surface, not for the whole company.** Split the product into parts with different
         needs: public and content pages (SEO, fast first paint on mobile), the account and admin areas (forms,
         grids, business rules), a highly interactive or offline client, widgets embedded in other sites. Each
         part may get its own decision.
      2. **What Blazor gives.** One language and one toolchain; models, validation rules and API contracts shared
         by server and client as .NET libraries; a team of .NET developers delivers a feature end to end. In a
         Blazor Web App (since .NET 8, including .NET 10) content pages are served with static server-side
         rendering and no client runtime, and interactivity is enabled per page or per component.
      3. **What Blazor costs.**
         - `InteractiveWebAssembly`: before the first interaction the browser downloads the .NET runtime and the
           app assemblies. Trimming, compression and caching reduce the size, but the first visit is usually
           heavier than for a typical JavaScript SPA, and AOT compilation speeds up execution at the price of an
           even larger download.
         - `InteractiveServer`: no download, but every UI event is a network round trip, the app needs a
           persistent connection, and the server keeps memory for every circuit.
         - Ecosystem: there are far fewer ready UI components than on npm. What remains are commercial component
           libraries or wrappers over JavaScript libraries through interop, and every wrapper must be maintained.
         - Hiring: the market has more frontend specialists with JavaScript/TypeScript experience than people with
           Blazor experience; on the other hand the company already has many .NET developers. Weigh this against
           the real team and the hiring plan.
      4. **Reduce long-term risk with architecture.** Both options age: JavaScript frameworks have major versions
         and build toolchain churn, Blazor moves with the yearly .NET releases (an LTS every two years) and depends
         on Microsoft's investment. So business logic and validation live outside UI components, and the server
         exposes a versioned HTTP API that any client can use: the UI of one surface can be rewritten without
         touching the backend. The technologies can coexist: Blazor calls JavaScript through interop, and Razor
         components can be rendered from a JavaScript app.
      5. **Decide on measurements and record the decision.** Prototype the hardest screens, measure first load on
         target devices and networks, interaction latency and development speed. Record the decision in an ADR
         with triggers for revisiting it: a change of audience, team composition or offline requirements.

      A typical result: the account and admin areas in Blazor, public pages with static server-side rendering,
      and a separate complex consumer client only where measurements and the team justify it.
    explanation: |
      The question is not which framework is "better" but which costs the product will pay for years. The benefit
      of shared C# code is large when the client holds a lot of logic: validation, calculations, complex forms. If
      the UI is a thin layer over an API, the benefit is small, and shared DTOs for TypeScript can be generated
      from an OpenAPI description.

      The price of WebAssembly is the size and time of the first download, and it hits hardest anonymous users on
      mobile networks, that is, public pages. For an internal area that an employee opens every day with the files
      already cached, the same price is barely noticeable. `InteractiveServer` removes the download but moves the
      cost to network latency and server memory. So one criterion weighs differently for different surfaces, and a
      single company-wide decision is almost always wrong for at least one of them.

      The ecosystem and the hiring market change more slowly than frameworks, so for a decision that lasts years
      they matter more than fashionable features. The main protection against a mistake is not guessing the right
      framework but making it replaceable: a clean API boundary and logic outside the UI let you rewrite one
      surface instead of the whole product. The render modes described here apply to Blazor Web Apps since .NET 8
      and hold for .NET 10.
    linkTitles:
      - "ASP.NET Core Blazor"
      - "ASP.NET Core Blazor hosting models"

    title: Which row of a Grid with RowDefinitions="Auto,*,Auto" gets the remaining page height in .NET MAUI?
    prompt: |
      A `Grid` fills the whole page and is declared with `RowDefinitions="Auto,*,Auto"`: the first row holds a
      `Label` header, the second a `CollectionView` list, and the third a `Button`.

      Which row gets all the page height that is left after the content is placed?
    hint: Which of the two sizing modes depends on the content of the row, and which depends on the space available to the `Grid` itself?

      b: "Row 1 with the `CollectionView`: the `*` row gets the height left after the two `Auto` rows."
      c: "Row 2 with the button: the last row stretches to the bottom of the page."
      d: The three rows split the page height equally.

      a: An `Auto` row gets exactly the height its content needs, here the height of the header. The order of the rows does not decide who gets the free space.
      c: The third row is also `Auto`, so its height is the height of the button. The button ends up at the bottom because the middle row took all the remaining space, not because the last row stretched.

    answer: "Row 1 with the `CollectionView`: the only `*` row gets all the height left after the `Auto` rows."
    explanation: |
      A `Grid` row height can be set in three ways: an absolute value in device-independent units, `Auto`, and
      `*` (star). An `Auto` row is sized to its content: here, the height of the header and the height of the
      button. Star rows share whatever is left after the absolute and `Auto` rows, in proportion to their
      factors.

      layout: the header sticks to the top, the button to the bottom, and the list fills everything between
      them and scrolls inside its row. With `Auto,2*,*` the free space would be split in a 2 to 1 ratio.

locales:
  ru:
    title: Через какие состояния проходит приложение .NET MAUI и какие события Window сопровождают переходы?
    prompt: |
      Код показывает класс `App`, который подписывается на события окна. Ответьте:

      - в каких состояниях выполнения может находиться приложение .NET MAUI;
      - какое событие `Window` возникает при каждом переходе между ними;
      - где на эти события подписываются и для чего их обычно используют.
    hint: Состояния отличаются тем, загружено ли приложение в память, видно ли окно и находится ли оно в фокусе.
    answer: |
      - **Состояния.** Не запущено (приложения нет в памяти), работает (окно видно и в фокусе), деактивировано
        (окно ещё видно, но потеряло фокус, например поверх него системный диалог), остановлено (окно не видно,
        приложение в фоне).
      - **Переходы и события:**
        - не запущено → работает: `Created`, затем `Activated`;
        - работает → деактивировано: `Deactivated`;
        - деактивировано → работает: `Activated`;
        - деактивировано → остановлено: `Stopped`;
        - остановлено → работает: `Resumed`; при первом запуске его нет, оно возможно только после `Stopped`;
        - остановлено → не запущено: `Destroying`.
      - **Где подписываться.** События принадлежат окну, а не приложению. Окно создаётся в переопределённом
        `App.CreateWindow`, там на него и подписываются, как в коде. Другой вариант - свой класс-наследник
        `Window` с переопределением `OnCreated`, `OnActivated`, `OnDeactivated`, `OnStopped`, `OnResumed` и
        `OnDestroying`.
      - **Для чего.** В `Stopped` сохраняют состояние и освобождают ресурсы: продолжения работы из этого состояния
        никто не гарантирует, ОС может завершить процесс. В `Resumed` обновляют данные, которые могли устареть,
        пока приложение было в фоне.
    explanation: |
      Каждая платформа описывает жизненный цикл по-своему: на Android это методы `Activity` (`OnResume`,
      `OnPause`, `OnStop` и другие), на iOS - методы делегата приложения. MAUI сводит их к четырём
      кроссплатформенным состояниям и шести событиям, чтобы общий код не зависел от платформы.

      События объявлены на `Window`, потому что приложение на десктопе или iPad может иметь несколько окон, и
      у каждого свой жизненный цикл.

      Важно различать похожие события. `Deactivated` не значит, что окно скрыто: оно может быть видно, просто
      без фокуса. `Activated` возникает и при первом запуске, и при каждом возврате фокуса, а `Resumed` - только
      при возврате из фона после `Stopped`. Поэтому обновление данных после фона кладут в `Resumed`, а не в
      `Activated`, иначе оно будет срабатывать на каждый закрытый системный диалог.

  en:
    title: Which states does a .NET MAUI app go through, and which Window events mark the transitions?
    prompt: |
      The code shows an `App` class that subscribes to window events. Answer:

      - which execution states a .NET MAUI app can be in;
      - which `Window` event is raised on each transition between them;
      - where you subscribe to these events and what they are usually used for.
    hint: The states differ in whether the app is loaded into memory, whether the window is visible and whether it has focus.
    answer: |
      - **States.** Not running (the app is not in memory), running (the window is visible and focused),
        deactivated (the window is still visible but has lost focus, for example a system dialog is on top of it),
        stopped (the window is not visible, the app is in the background).
      - **Transitions and events:**
        - not running → running: `Created`, then `Activated`;
        - running → deactivated: `Deactivated`;
        - deactivated → running: `Activated`;
        - deactivated → stopped: `Stopped`;
        - stopped → running: `Resumed`; it is not raised on first launch, only after `Stopped`;
        - stopped → not running: `Destroying`.
      - **Where to subscribe.** The events belong to the window, not to the application. The window is created in
        an overridden `App.CreateWindow`, and that is where you subscribe, as in the code. Another option is a
        class derived from `Window` that overrides `OnCreated`, `OnActivated`, `OnDeactivated`, `OnStopped`,
        `OnResumed` and `OnDestroying`.
      - **What for.** In `Stopped` you save state and release resources: nothing guarantees that the app resumes
        from this state, the OS may terminate the process. In `Resumed` you refresh data that may have gone stale
        while the app was in the background.
    explanation: |
      Each platform describes its lifecycle in its own way: on Android these are `Activity` methods (`OnResume`,
      `OnPause`, `OnStop` and others), on iOS the methods of the app delegate. MAUI maps them to four
      cross-platform states and six events, so that shared code does not depend on the platform.

      The events are declared on `Window` because an app on desktop or iPad can have several windows, and each
      has its own lifecycle.

      It matters to tell similar events apart. `Deactivated` does not mean the window is hidden: it can still be
      visible, just without focus. `Activated` is raised on first launch and every time focus comes back, while
      `Resumed` is raised only on the return from the background after `Stopped`. That is why a refresh after
      the background goes into `Resumed`, not `Activated`; otherwise it would run after every dismissed system
      dialog.
    linkTitles:
      - ".NET MAUI app lifecycle"
      - "Windows in .NET MAUI"

    title: Что нужно сделать, чтобы Shell.GoToAsync открыл страницу, которой нет в AppShell.xaml?
    prompt: |
      В приложении .NET MAUI на Shell есть страница списка заказов, объявленная в `AppShell.xaml`.
      Страница деталей `OrderDetailsPage` в `AppShell.xaml` не объявлена. При нажатии на заказ вызывается

      по маршруту узнаёт тип страницы, а если этот тип есть в контейнере, создаёт его через контейнер с

  en:
    title: What must you do so that Shell.GoToAsync opens a page that is not declared in AppShell.xaml?
    prompt: |
      A Shell-based .NET MAUI app has an order list page declared in `AppShell.xaml`. The detail page
      `OrderDetailsPage` is not declared in `AppShell.xaml`. Tapping an order calls
      `await Shell.Current.GoToAsync("orderdetails");`.

      What must be done beforehand so that this call opens `OrderDetailsPage`?
    hint: How does Shell learn which page type matches a route string when the page is not in the visual hierarchy?
    options:
      a: Nothing, Shell finds the page by its class name `OrderDetailsPage`.
      b: 'Register the route: `Routing.RegisterRoute("orderdetails", typeof(OrderDetailsPage))`, usually in the `AppShell` constructor.'
      c: Register the page only in the dependency injection container with `builder.Services.AddTransient<OrderDetailsPage>()`.
      d: 'Navigate to the absolute route `"//orderdetails"` instead of the relative one.'
      e: Open the page once with `Navigation.PushAsync(new OrderDetailsPage())`, after which Shell knows the route.
    optionExplanations:
      a: Shell does not look pages up by class name. A route string must be tied to a page type explicitly, either in the visual hierarchy or with `Routing.RegisterRoute`.
      c: Registering in the container lets Shell create the page with injected dependencies, but it does not create a route. Without `Routing.RegisterRoute` the string `orderdetails` is still tied to nothing.
      d: Absolute routes with `//` lead to pages of the Shell visual hierarchy. A global detail-page route cannot be the only page on the navigation stack, so absolute navigation to it is not supported, and the registration is still needed.
      e: '`PushAsync` just puts a page instance on the navigation stack and registers no route. The next `GoToAsync("orderdetails")` call still cannot find the route.'
    answer: 'Register the route with `Routing.RegisterRoute("orderdetails", typeof(OrderDetailsPage))` before navigating, usually in the `AppShell` constructor.'
    explanation: |
      Shell has two sources of routes. Pages of the visual hierarchy (`FlyoutItem`, `Tab`, `ShellContent`) get
      their routes from `AppShell.xaml`, for example through the `Route` property. Detail pages that are not in
      the hierarchy are registered as global routes with `Routing.RegisterRoute`, which ties a route string to a
      page type.

      The registration must run before the first navigation, which is why it usually lives in the `AppShell`
      constructor. After that the relative navigation `GoToAsync("orderdetails")` creates `OrderDetailsPage` and
      pushes it onto the navigation stack of the current tab. If the route is not registered, Shell cannot map
      the string to a page type, and the navigation ends with an exception.

      Registering the page in the dependency injection container complements route registration, it does not
      replace it: the route tells Shell the page type, and if that type is in the container, Shell creates it
      through the container with its dependencies injected.
    linkTitles:
      - ".NET MAUI Shell navigation"
      - "Dependency injection in .NET MAUI"

    title: Which .NET MAUI control properties bind in TwoWay mode by default?
    prompt: |
      In the XAML of a .NET MAUI page the bindings are written without `Mode`, for example `Text="{Binding Name}"`.
      Select all properties that then work in `TwoWay` mode, that is, pass changes not only from the view model
      to the control but also from the control back to the view model.
    hint: Which of these properties can the user change by interacting with the control?
    options:
      a: "`Entry.Text`"
      b: "`Slider.Value`"
      c: "`Switch.IsToggled`"
      d: "`Label.Text`"
    optionExplanations:
      d: '`Label` only displays text and the user does not edit it, so `Label.Text` binds in `OneWay` mode by default: changes flow from the view model to the control.'
    answer: "`Entry.Text`, `Slider.Value` and `Switch.IsToggled`."
    explanation: |
      The default binding mode is set not by the binding but by the bindable property itself: when it is declared
      with `BindableProperty.Create`, the `defaultBindingMode` parameter is given. If a binding has no `Mode`
      (or `BindingMode.Default`), the mode of the property is used.

      Most bindable properties default to `OneWay`. The exceptions are properties whose value the user enters:
      `Entry.Text`, `Slider.Value`, `Switch.IsToggled` and similar ones (`Editor.Text`, `DatePicker.Date`,
      `Stepper.Value`). They default to `TwoWay`, so that user input reaches the view model without an explicit
      `Mode=TwoWay`. `Label.Text` only shows data, so it stays `OneWay`.

      The practical consequence: if an `Entry` should only show a value and never change the view model property,
      `Mode=OneWay` must be set explicitly. For a property that defaults to `TwoWay`, the source property needs an
      accessible setter, otherwise the value cannot be passed back.
    linkTitles:
      - "Binding mode in .NET MAUI"
      - "Bindable properties in .NET MAUI"

      when the user signs out.

    title: How do you inject view models and services into .NET MAUI pages, and which lifetime should they get?
    prompt: |
      A Shell-based .NET MAUI (.NET 10) app has an `OrderDetailsPage` page with an `OrderDetailsViewModel` view
      model that needs an `IOrderService` service.

      How do you get the view model and services into the page constructor through dependency injection? Who
      creates the page when Shell navigates to a route? Which lifetime do you choose for pages, view models and
      services, and what goes wrong with a bad choice?
    hint: Who creates the page object when Shell navigates to a route, and what happens to its state when the user opens the page a second time?
    answer: |
      - **Registration.** In `MauiProgram.CreateMauiApp`, through `builder.Services`: `AddSingleton<IOrderService, OrderService>()`,
        `AddTransient<OrderDetailsViewModel>()`, `AddTransient<OrderDetailsPage>()`. The page takes the view model
        in its constructor and assigns it to `BindingContext`; the view model takes `IOrderService`.
      - **Who creates the page.** Shell creates pages from `ShellContent` (`ContentTemplate="{DataTemplate local:OrdersPage}"`)
        and route pages from `Routing.RegisterRoute` through the container when the page type is registered in it.
        The whole dependency chain is resolved automatically. Do not create such a page with `new`: the container
        is then bypassed. Without Shell (`NavigationPage`) you have to get the page from the container yourself,
        for example by injecting it or a factory into the previous page.
      - **Lifetimes.**
        - Services with shared state or that are expensive to create (API client, settings, cache) - singleton.
        - Detail pages and their view models - transient: every navigation gets a new instance without the
          previous order's data, and a closed page can be collected by the garbage collector.
        - Root tab pages can be singletons, but Shell creates a `ShellContent` page once and keeps it anyway.
        - Scoped has no request boundary in MAUI as it does in ASP.NET Core: a scope is created per window, so in
          a single-window app such a service lives almost like a singleton.
      - **Pitfalls.** A singleton that depends on a transient captures it for the whole lifetime of the app. A
        singleton page or view model shows stale state and accumulates subscriptions to events of long-lived
        services. Reaching into the container through `IPlatformApplication.Current.Services` is a last resort,
        not the main approach.
    explanation: |
      .NET MAUI uses the same `Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection` container as ASP.NET Core, and
      `MauiApp.CreateBuilder()` exposes it through `builder.Services`. Constructor injection makes the
      dependencies of the page and the view model explicit: the view model can be tested without a device by
      passing a fake `IOrderService`.

      The key point is who creates the page. When Shell creates it from a registered type, the container resolves
      its constructor and everything it needs. When code creates the page with `new`, injection does not happen,
      and the developer starts pulling services out of the container by hand.

      Lifetime matters more in a mobile app than it seems: pages and view models live long, and a singleton
      detail page means the user sees the previous order on the next visit, while the view model's subscriptions
      to service events are never released. Transient for pages and view models that hold screen state, and
      singleton for shared services, is a sensible default. The answer holds for .NET MAUI in .NET 10.

      - "Dependency injection in .NET MAUI"
      - ".NET MAUI Shell navigation"

    title: Когда в .NET MAUI использовать #if ANDROID, а когда разделяемые классы в папках Platforms?
    prompt: |
      В едином проекте .NET MAUI нужна платформенная функциональность, например определить ориентацию устройства
      через нативные API Android и iOS. Есть два способа: блоки условной компиляции `#if ANDROID` / `#if IOS`
      прямо в общем коде и разделяемые (`partial`) классы, у которых общая часть лежит в общем коде, а реализации -
      в папках `Platforms/Android`, `Platforms/iOS` и так далее.

      Как каждый способ работает при сборке, в чём их сильные и слабые стороны и когда вы выберете тот или другой?
    hint: Что именно попадает в сборку под Android и что видит разработчик, который читает общий класс?
    answer: |
      - **Как собирается единый проект.** Проект нацелен на несколько платформенных целевых фреймворков
        (`-android`, `-ios`, `-maccatalyst`, `-windows`) и собирается отдельно под каждый. В каждой такой сборке
        определён свой символ (`ANDROID`, `IOS`, `MACCATALYST`, `WINDOWS`), а файлы из папки `Platforms/<платформа>`
        компилируются только для своей платформы. Оба способа работают на этапе компиляции.
      - **Условная компиляция.** Код внутри `#if ANDROID` попадает только в сборку под Android. Это удобно для
        нескольких строк: один вызов нативного API, нужный `using`, регистрация сервиса в `MauiProgram`, общий
        для двух платформ фрагмент `#if IOS || MACCATALYST`. Минусы: платформенные ветки расползаются по общему
        коду, класс трудно читать, а неактивные ветки компилятор проверяет только при сборке под их платформу,
        поэтому ошибка в ветке iOS видна лишь при сборке под iOS.
      - **Разделяемые классы.** В общем коде объявляется API, например
        `public partial class DeviceOrientationService` с методом `public partial DeviceOrientation GetOrientation();`.
        В `Platforms/Android` и `Platforms/iOS` лежат файлы с той же частью класса и реализацией метода. Имя класса
        и пространство имён должны совпадать: файл в папке платформы по умолчанию получает пространство имён по
        пути, его нужно привести к общему. Вызывающий код видит один API без единого `#if`, а сборка берёт только
        реализацию целевой платформы.
      - **Подводный камень разделяемых методов.** Метод с модификатором доступа обязан иметь реализацию в каждой
        сборке. Если для какой-то цели её нет (платформа без файла или дополнительный целевой фреймворк без
        платформы, например для модульных тестов), сборка падает с ошибкой CS8795. Нужна реализация-заглушка
        или условие в файле проекта.
      - **Как выбирать.** Несколько строк в одном месте - `#if`. Заметная логика, несколько членов, несколько
        платформ - разделяемый класс. Если реализацию нужно подменять в тестах, лучше интерфейс и по одной
        реализации на платформу, а выбор регистрации в `MauiProgram` - короткий `#if`. Если раскладка по папкам
        неудобна, можно настроить мультитаргетинг по суффиксам имён файлов (`*.Android.cs`) условиями `Compile Remove`
        в файле проекта.
      - **Проверка во время выполнения не заменяет эти способы.** Условие `DeviceInfo.Platform == DevicePlatform.Android`
        не поможет вызвать нативный API: типы вроде `Android.Content.Context` не существуют в сборке под iOS, и код
        просто не скомпилируется без разделения на этапе сборки.
    explanation: |
      Оба способа решают одну задачу: в сборку под конкретную платформу должен попасть только код, который
      компилируется против её нативных API. Разница в организации кода. Условная компиляция держит все платформы
      в одном файле, поэтому она дешёвая для точечных вставок, но с ростом числа веток общий класс превращается в
      набор платформенных фрагментов, которые никто не видит целиком.

      Разделяемые классы отделяют контракт от реализаций: общий код зависит от одного API, а каждая платформа
      реализует его в своём файле. Это проще читать и сопровождать, а отсутствующая реализация обнаруживается
      ошибкой компиляции, а не поведением во время выполнения. Цена - больше файлов и требование реализовать
      метод для каждой цели сборки, включая цели без платформы.

      Интерфейс с реализациями по платформам добавляет к этому возможность подменить зависимость в тестах и
      внедрить её через DI, поэтому для сервисов, которые использует модель представления, он часто удобнее
      разделяемого класса.
    linkTitles:
      - "Вызов платформенного кода в .NET MAUI"
      - "Настройка мультитаргетинга в .NET MAUI"
  en:
    title: When should a .NET MAUI app use #if ANDROID, and when partial classes in the Platforms folders?
    prompt: |
      A single .NET MAUI project needs platform-specific functionality, for example reading the device orientation
      through native Android and iOS APIs. There are two ways: conditional compilation blocks `#if ANDROID` /
      `#if IOS` directly in shared code, and `partial` classes whose shared part lives in shared code while the
      implementations live in the `Platforms/Android`, `Platforms/iOS` and other platform folders.

      How does each approach work at build time, what are their strengths and weaknesses, and when do you choose each?
    hint: What exactly goes into the Android build, and what does a developer see when reading the shared class?
    answer: |
      - **How a single project builds.** The project targets several platform target frameworks (`-android`, `-ios`,
        `-maccatalyst`, `-windows`) and is built separately for each. Each build defines its own symbol (`ANDROID`,
        `IOS`, `MACCATALYST`, `WINDOWS`), and the files in `Platforms/<platform>` are compiled only for that platform.
        Both approaches work at compile time.
      - **Conditional compilation.** Code inside `#if ANDROID` goes only into the Android build. It suits a few lines:
        one native API call, a required `using`, a service registration in `MauiProgram`, a fragment shared by two
        platforms with `#if IOS || MACCATALYST`. The downsides: platform branches spread through shared code, the class
        becomes hard to read, and the compiler checks inactive branches only when building for their platform, so a
        mistake in the iOS branch shows up only in the iOS build.
      - **Partial classes.** Shared code declares the API, for example `public partial class DeviceOrientationService`
        with the method `public partial DeviceOrientation GetOrientation();`. `Platforms/Android` and `Platforms/iOS`
        hold files with the same class part and the method implementation. The class name and namespace must match:
        a file in a platform folder gets a path-based namespace by default, and it has to be aligned with the shared
        one. Callers see one API without a single `#if`, and the build takes only the target platform's implementation.
      - **The partial method pitfall.** A method with an access modifier must have an implementation in every build.
        If some target lacks it (a platform without a file, or an extra target framework without a platform, for
        example one used for unit tests), the build fails with error CS8795. You need a stub implementation or a
        condition in the project file.
      - **How to choose.** A few lines in one place: `#if`. Substantial logic, several members, several platforms: a
        partial class. If the implementation must be replaced in tests, prefer an interface with one implementation per
        platform, and pick the registration in `MauiProgram` with a short `#if`. If the folder layout is inconvenient,
        you can set up multi-targeting by file name suffix (`*.Android.cs`) with `Compile Remove` conditions in the
        project file.
      - **A runtime check does not replace them.** The condition `DeviceInfo.Platform == DevicePlatform.Android` does
        not let you call a native API: types such as `Android.Content.Context` do not exist in the iOS build, so the
        code does not compile without separation at build time.
    explanation: |
      Both approaches solve the same problem: the build for a given platform must contain only code that compiles
      against that platform's native APIs. The difference is how the code is organized. Conditional compilation keeps
      all platforms in one file, so it is cheap for small insertions, but as branches grow the shared class turns into
      a set of platform fragments that nobody sees as a whole.

      Partial classes separate the contract from the implementations: shared code depends on one API, and each
      platform implements it in its own file. This is easier to read and maintain, and a missing implementation is a
      compile error rather than runtime behaviour. The cost is more files and the requirement to implement the method
      for every build target, including targets without a platform.

      An interface with per-platform implementations adds the ability to replace the dependency in tests and inject
      it through DI, so for services used by a view model it is often more convenient than a partial class.
    linkTitles:
      - "Invoke platform code in .NET MAUI"
      - "Configure multi-targeting in .NET MAUI"

  en:
    title: How do the //orders, .., ../details and details routes work in .NET MAUI Shell navigation?
    prompt: |
      `AppShell` declares a `ShellContent` with the route `orders`, and the order detail page is registered in code
      as `details` (see the code). Which statements about the `GoToAsync` calls are true? Select all that apply.
    hint: Compare the routes with file system paths, and remember how a page registered in code differs from an element of the Shell visual hierarchy.
    options:
      a: "The route `//orders` is absolute: Shell goes to `orders` in the visual hierarchy and replaces the navigation stack instead of pushing a page on top of the current one."
      b: "The route `../details` keeps the current page on the stack and pushes `details` on top of it: `..` only marks the path as relative."
      c: "The route `..` navigates back: it pops one page from the navigation stack."
      d: "The route `//details` opens the detail page as the only page on the stack, even though it is registered only with `Routing.RegisterRoute`."
      e: "The route `details` is searched relative to the current position, and the matching page is pushed onto the current navigation stack."
      f: "No parameters can be passed with the `..` route, so the only way to return data to the previous page is a messenger or a shared service."
    optionExplanations:
      b: "`..` in a route is a step back. Shell first pops the current page and only then pushes `details`, so the current page leaves the stack."
      d: "A global route registered with `Routing.RegisterRoute` cannot be the only page on the stack, so absolute navigation to it is not supported. An absolute route must lead to an element of the Shell visual hierarchy."
      f: "Parameters can be passed when navigating back too: in a query string (`..?name=value`) or in a dictionary as the second argument of `GoToAsync`. The previous page receives them the same way as with forward navigation."
    answer: "a, c and e are true: `//orders` replaces the navigation stack, `..` pops one page, and the relative route `details` pushes the page onto the current stack."
    explanation: |
      A route prefix decides two things: where the route is searched from and what happens to the navigation stack.

      - `route` - searched upwards from the current position, the matching page is pushed onto the stack.
      - `/route` - searched downwards from the current position, the page is pushed onto the stack.
      - `//route` - searched upwards from the current position, the matching page replaces the stack.
      - `///route` - searched downwards from the current position, the page replaces the stack.

      `..` navigates back one page, and it can be combined with a route: `../details` pops the current page and pushes
      `details`, `../../details` pops two. This is a convenient way to replace one page with another without piling
      up extra entries on the stack.

      In practice an absolute route switches a section of the app, for example after sign-in or when moving to another
      tab with a cleared stack. A relative route suits drilling into details, and `..` suits returning, including with
      a result passed as parameters. The limit of absolute routes is that they lead only to elements of the visual
      hierarchy: a page registered in code cannot become the root of the stack.
    linkTitles:
      - "Shell navigation in .NET MAUI"

  en:
    title: Where should a .NET MAUI page load its data, and what changes when the user comes back from a detail page?
    prompt: |
      The order list page loads its data as shown in the code. `LoadOrdersAsync` clears the `Orders` collection
      and refills it with the server response. Users complain: after they come back from an order page the list
      flickers, the scroll position jumps to the top, and the server logs show an extra request for every tap on
      "Back".

      Explain when the page constructor, `OnAppearing` and `OnNavigatedTo` run, where to start loading data,
      and how to make the page refresh its data on return only when that is really needed.
    hint: How many times is an instance created for a page that stays in the navigation stack under the detail page, and how many times does it become visible?
    answer: |
      - **The constructor** runs once per page instance. The list page stays in the stack under the detail page,
        so going back creates no new instance and the constructor does not run. In Shell the page of a root
        `ShellContent` is created once and reused, while a route page registered in DI as transient is created
        again on every forward navigation to it.
      - **Starting async loading in the constructor** is awkward: you cannot `await` it, task errors are easy
        to lose, there is nothing to tie cancellation to, and Shell navigation parameters are not applied yet.
      - **`OnAppearing`** runs every time the page becomes visible: on the first display, on return from the
        detail page, when the user switches to its tab.
      - **`OnNavigatedTo`** runs when the page becomes the target of navigation, including back navigation. It
        repeats too, but it is tied to navigation rather than visibility.
      - **The cause of the symptoms.** The code in the example repeats the load on every "Back". Clearing and
        refilling the collection recreates the list items, hence the flicker, the scroll reset and the extra
        request.
      - **The first load.** Start it in `OnAppearing` or `OnNavigatedTo` (the page is already on screen, so you
        can show a busy indicator), but guard it against repeats: a flag in the view model that is set after a
        successful load, or a stored task of the first load, so that a second call does not start another load.
      - **Deliberate refresh.** If the detail page changed the order, return the result:
        `Shell.Current.GoToAsync("..", parameters)` and receive it in `IQueryAttributable.ApplyQueryAttributes`,
        or send a message through a messenger. Then update one item, not the whole list. For a refresh the user
        asks for, use `RefreshView` (pull-to-refresh) or a check of the data age.
      - **Robustness.** The `OnAppearing` override returns `void`, so an `async` version is `async void`: wrap
        the body in `try/catch` and show an error state, otherwise an exception crashes the app. If the user
        leaves the page, cancel an unfinished load with a `CancellationToken` in `OnDisappearing` or
        `OnNavigatedFrom`.
    explanation: |
      The constructor and `OnAppearing` answer different questions: "when was the page object created" and
      "when is the page on screen again". With stack navigation the page under the detail page is not destroyed,
      it is only covered. When the top page is popped, the page below becomes visible again and gets
      `OnAppearing` and `OnNavigatedTo`, but its instance, its view model and the data it already loaded stay
      the same.

      So an unconditional load in `OnAppearing` does not mean "load the page data", it means "reload it on every
      display". Sometimes that is what you want, but then it should be a decision, not a side effect. Usually it
      is better to load the data once and pass changes from the detail page back precisely: Shell lets you pass
      data on backward navigation with `..` as well.

      The constructor is a poor place to start loading not because it runs rarely, but because it cannot
      properly await an async operation and handle its error, and navigation parameters are not there yet.

      - "ContentPage in .NET MAUI"
      - ".NET MAUI Shell navigation"

      gone.

      Which `Window` event, subscribed to from code shared across platforms, is the reliable place to persist
      the draft so that it survives such a process termination?
    hint: Which events can the app still count on after it goes to the background, if the operating system later decides to free memory?
    options:
      a: "`Destroying`"
      b: "`Stopped`"
      c: "`Resumed`"
      d: "`Created`"
      e: "`Backgrounding`"

      a: "`Destroying` is raised when the native window is destroyed in an orderly way. The system can terminate a background process without it, and the draft is lost."
      c: "`Resumed` is raised on return from the stopped state. If the process was terminated in the background there is no return, the app starts from scratch."

      The documentation warns explicitly that the app may never resume from this state: the operating system
      may terminate the process to free memory, and no event is raised before that. So `Stopped` is the last
      point where the code is guaranteed to get control, and the draft must be saved there.

      the process in the background. Code that saves state only there works on a normal window close and loses
      data in exactly the scenario users complain about.

      the window loses focus and stays visible. A robust scheme saves the draft during editing with a debounce,

      editor opens. Do not start long operations such as uploading to a server in the `Stopped` handler: the
      system does not have to wait for them to finish.

      `Window` subclass by overriding `OnStopped`.

    title: Почему в Release-сборке .NET MAUI для iOS с обрезкой часть привязок остаётся пустой и как это исправить, не отключая обрезку?
    prompt: |

  en:
    title: Why do some bindings stay empty in a trimmed iOS Release build of a .NET MAUI app, and how do you fix it without disabling trimming?
    prompt: |
      A .NET MAUI app works correctly in Debug. In the Release build for iOS, where the project sets
      `TrimMode` to `full`, some labels on several pages stay empty. There are no exceptions and no crashes.
      The XAML uses plain `{Binding PropertyName}` bindings without `x:DataType`.

      Explain why this happens only in Release, how to fix it without turning trimming off, and how to keep it
      from coming back.
    hint: How does the trimmer learn that a property is used if the only access to it is a string name resolved at run time?
    answer: |
      - **Why Debug works.** In Debug the app code is not trimmed: its assemblies ship whole, so a binding that
        looks up a property through reflection at run time always finds it.
      - **Why Release breaks.** The trimmer (ILLink) does static analysis and keeps only what IL references.
        `{Binding Title}` without `x:DataType` is just a string path resolved through reflection at run time, so
        nothing in IL references the getter of `Title`. If no C# code reads that property, the trimmer may remove
        the getter or the whole member. The binding then finds nothing and silently keeps the default value:
        binding failures in MAUI throw no exceptions, so the symptom is an empty field.
      - **The main fix is compiled bindings.** Set `x:DataType` on the page (the view model type) and on every
        `DataTemplate` (the item type). The XAML compiler turns such a binding into code that accesses the
        property directly, the trimmer sees the reference and keeps the member. Write bindings created in C#
        with the lambda overloads added in .NET 9, for example
        `label.SetBinding(Label.TextProperty, static (OrderViewModel vm) => vm.Title)`, not with string paths.
      - **Find what is left.** Since .NET 9 the XAML compiler warns about bindings that could be compiled
        (`XC0022`, `XC0023`), and the trimmer reports trim analysis warnings (for example `IL2026`) for reflection
        it cannot analyse. Treat these warnings as errors in the Release build, so a new string binding breaks
        the build instead of a screen.
      - **What cannot be compiled.** For the few places where reflection stays (a dynamic context with
        `x:DataType="{x:Null}"`, code that reads properties by name), keep the members explicitly:
        `[DynamicDependency]` or `[DynamicallyAccessedMembers]` on the code that uses reflection, or a root
        descriptor for a specific type. Rooting a whole assembly with `TrimmerRootAssembly` is a last resort.
        Turning trimming off only hides the defect and makes the package larger.
      - **Lock it in.** Run UI smoke tests on a Release build on a device or simulator in CI: Debug never shows
        this class of bugs.
    explanation: |
      Trimming is static analysis: ILLink starts from the entry points, follows references in IL and removes
      everything it does not reach. Access through reflection by a string name is invisible to that analysis,
      which is why the .NET MAUI trimming documentation lists reflection-based bindings among the features that
      are incompatible with full trimming. Debug hides the defect because there the app code is not trimmed and
      every property is still in the assembly.

      A compiled binding removes the cause, not the symptom: with `x:DataType` the XAML compiler resolves the
      path at build time and generates code that calls the property getter, which is an ordinary reference for
      the trimmer. As a bonus a wrong path becomes a build error, and the binding is faster because it does not
      use reflection. Preservation attributes and descriptors are a targeted complement for code that really
      needs reflection, not a replacement for compiled bindings.

      The behaviour described holds for .NET 10. Compiled bindings in C# through lambdas and the `XC0022` and
      `XC0023` warnings appeared in .NET 9.
    linkTitles:
      - "Trim a .NET MAUI app"
      - "Compiled bindings in .NET MAUI"

    title: Which practices reduce the measure and arrange cost of a complex .NET MAUI page?
    prompt: |
      A complex .NET MAUI order form page opens slowly, and profiling shows that a noticeable share of the time
      goes to layout passes: measuring and arranging elements.
      Which changes reduce this work? Select all that apply.
    hint: What does the layout engine have to do for every extra nesting level and for every row whose size depends on its content?
    options:

      b: "Remove a layout that holds a single child and place that child directly in the parent"
      c: "In a `Grid`, give rows and columns whose size does not have to follow their content a fixed or star (`*`) size instead of `Auto`"

    answer: "Replace nested stacks with one `Grid`, remove layouts that hold a single child, and avoid `Auto` where the size does not need to depend on content."
    explanation: |
      Every layout first measures its children and then arranges them. Nested layouts repeat these passes on
      every level, and a size change deep in the tree invalidates the measurements of its chain of ancestors.
      Fewer levels means less work.

      - One `Grid` places many elements on one level, while imitating a grid with nested stacks creates extra
        levels and extra calculations.
      - A layout designed for several children that holds only one is pure overhead.
      - An `Auto` row or column cannot be sized without measuring its content, which is additional calculation.
        A fixed size is known at once, and `*` divides the remaining space proportionally.

      Extra wrappers and `Center` alignment on every layout do not cut the work: they add to it or get in the
      way of optimization.

  en:
    title: When does Shell fit a .NET MAUI app better than NavigationPage, and what does Shell constrain?
    prompt: |
      A team starts a .NET MAUI app and has to choose a navigation model: `Shell` or a page stack built on
      `NavigationPage`. Explain what each model gives you, which apps Shell suits better, what constraints it
      imposes, and whether the two models can be combined in one app.
    hint: Compare who owns the app structure and the page stack in each model, and how each model addresses the page you want to open.
    answer: |
      - **What Shell gives.** The app structure is described once in `AppShell.xaml`: flyout, bottom and top
        tabs (`FlyoutItem`, `TabBar`, `Tab`, `ShellContent`). Navigation is URI-based: routes from the hierarchy
        and detail page routes registered with `Routing.RegisterRoute`, navigation with
        `Shell.Current.GoToAsync("orders/details")`, absolute routes with `//`, going back with `..`. Parameters
        travel in a query string or an `IDictionary<string, object>` and are received through
        `IQueryAttributable` or `[QueryProperty]`. Pages are created on demand from a `DataTemplate`, and if the
        page type is registered in the DI container, Shell resolves it from the container together with its
        constructor dependencies. The `Navigating` event lets you cancel navigation, and `BackButtonBehavior`
        overrides the back button.
      - **When Shell fits better.** An app with a typical flyout or tab structure, many screens, a need for deep
        links, view models that navigate by string routes without knowing page types, and pages that get their
        dependencies through DI.
      - **What Shell constrains.** The hierarchy is fixed: `Shell` -> `FlyoutItem` or `TabBar` -> `Tab` ->
        `ShellContent`, a `ShellContent` holds a `ContentPage`, and there are at most two levels of tabs (bottom
        and top). The look of the flyout and the tab bar is customizable within attached properties and
        templates; beyond that you need platform code. `TabbedPage` and `FlyoutPage` are not supported inside
        Shell, and `NavigationPage` is not needed: every tab has its own stack. Root `ShellContent` pages are
        created once and live as long as the Shell, so a `Transient` registration does not recreate them. Routes
        are strings, and a typo in a route shows up only at run time.
      - **What NavigationPage gives.** A page stack that code controls explicitly: `PushAsync`, `PopAsync`,
        `PopToRootAsync`, `InsertPageBefore`, `RemovePage`, and modal `PushModalAsync`. There are no routes: the
        code creates the page itself (or resolves it from the container explicitly) and passes data through the
        constructor or properties. `NavigationPage` combines freely with `TabbedPage` and `FlyoutPage`, for
        example one stack per tab.
      - **When NavigationPage fits better.** A small app with a linear stack or a step-by-step wizard; a root
        structure that the Shell hierarchy cannot express; code that rebuilds the stack a lot; moving a
        Xamarin.Forms app built on `NavigationPage` without rewriting its navigation.
      - **Do not nest one model in the other.** Pick one model for the window root. Replacing the root as a
        whole is fine, for example assigning a new `AppShell` to `Window.Page` after sign-in, or keeping a
        separate `//login` route with the flyout disabled inside Shell itself. In .NET 9 and .NET 10 the root
        page is set through `CreateWindow`, and `Application.MainPage` is marked obsolete.
    explanation: |
      Shell is a ready-made app container with opinions about structure: it builds the flyout, the tabs and the
      stacks itself and decides which page to create for a route. A route decouples the calling code from the
      page type, which is what makes deep links, navigation from a view model without references to
      `Microsoft.Maui.Controls`, and page creation through DI possible. The price is a hierarchy you cannot
      reshape freely and string routes that are not checked at build time.

      `NavigationPage` is a primitive: one stack and full manual control. You choose it when the Shell
      structure gets in the way more than it helps, and when manual control of the stack is a requirement
      rather than an inconvenience.

      Mixing the models under one root is a bad idea because both keep their own stack and their own back
      button, and the Shell navigation bar starts fighting the nested `NavigationPage` bar. The .NET 9 and
      .NET 10 behaviour is described as of .NET 10.
    linkTitles:
      - "Shell in .NET MAUI"
      - "NavigationPage in .NET MAUI"
      - "Shell navigation"

    prompt: |
      Пользователи жалуются, что приложение на .NET MAUI со временем тормозит и падает на слабых Android-
      телефонах. Вы замечаете: каждый раз, когда пользователь открывает страницу деталей заказа
      `OrderDetailPage` и возвращается назад, память процесса вырастает на несколько мегабайт и не
      возвращается. Страница использует `OrderDetailViewModel`, внедрённую через DI.

      Как вы найдёте, что удерживает страницу, и в каком порядке будете действовать?
    hint: Что должно произойти со страницей после возврата назад, и какой объект может жить дольше неё и при этом знать о ней?
    answer: |
      1. **Убедиться, что это утечка, а не задержка сборки.** Открыть и закрыть страницу 10-20 раз в
         Release-сборке без отладчика (Hot Reload и инструменты XAML в Debug могут держать лишние ссылки),
         затем вызвать полную сборку мусора. Рост, который исчезает после полной сборки, - не утечка.
      2. **Доказать, что страница не собирается.** В отладочном коде сохранить `WeakReference` на страницу и
         на модель представления при уходе со страницы, после возврата вызвать
         `GC.Collect(); GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers(); GC.Collect();` и проверить `IsAlive`. Проверять отдельно
         страницу, модель и подозрительные дочерние элементы: так поиск сужается.
      3. **Снять дампы кучи.** `dotnet-gcdump collect` до и после серии открытий; на Android и iOS -
         через `dotnet-dsrouter`, на Windows и Mac Catalyst - напрямую. Сравнить дампы в Visual Studio или
         PerfView: растёт число экземпляров `OrderDetailPage` и `OrderDetailViewModel`. Для выжившего
         экземпляра смотреть путь до корня - он и показывает, кто держит страницу.
      4. **Проверить типичные корни.**

         - страница или модель зарегистрированы как `Singleton` или сохранены в статическом поле, либо

    explanation: |
      Страница, из которой вернулись назад, больше не достижима из визуального дерева, и сборщик мусора должен
      её освободить. Если она жива, значит на неё ведёт цепочка ссылок от корня: статического поля, синглтона

      нативные представления и картинки. Поэтому каждое посещение и добавляет мегабайты.

      Порядок важен. Сначала надо отличить утечку от отложенной сборки: старшее поколение собирается редко, и
      рост памяти сам по себе ничего не доказывает. `WeakReference` после принудительной сборки даёт быстрый
      ответ «собирается или нет», а дамп кучи - путь до корня, то есть конкретную строку кода, которую надо

    prompt: |
