    title: Чем рискуют позиционные записи в роли общих контрактов в NuGet-пакетах и как спроектировать их для эволюции?
    prompt: |
      Позиционные записи вроде `OrderPlaced` лежат в общем NuGet-пакете `Shop.Contracts` и служат сообщениями и DTO
      для десятков сервисов, которые будут жить с этим пакетом годами. Сервисы и другие пакеты собираются и
      развёртываются независимо.

      В версии 1.1.0 команда хочет добавить валюту:
      `public record OrderPlaced(Guid OrderId, decimal Amount, string Currency = "EUR");`

      - Что сломается у потребителей вроде `BillingHandler` и в какой форме: при компиляции или во время выполнения?
      - Какие ещё изменения позиционных параметров опасны?
      - Как спроектировать такие контракты, чтобы они могли развиваться, и что закрепить в процессе?
    hint: "Какие публичные члены компилятор создаёт из одного позиционного параметра, и по чему CLR находит конструктор, который вызывает уже собранная сборка?"
    answer: |
      1. **Что попадает в публичный API.** Каждый позиционный параметр компилятор превращает сразу в несколько
         публичных членов: параметр основного конструктора, свойство `init` с тем же именем, параметр `out`
         синтезированного метода `Deconstruct` (на нём же работают позиционные шаблоны вроде `OrderPlaced(_, > 1000m)`)
         и часть `Equals`, `GetHashCode` и `ToString`. Порядок и типы параметров становятся частью сигнатур.
      2. **Добавление параметра, даже со значением по умолчанию.**
         - Конструктор `OrderPlaced(Guid, decimal)` исчезает, вместо него появляется `OrderPlaced(Guid, decimal, string)`.
           Значение по умолчанию компилятор подставляет в точку вызова, поэтому `new OrderPlaced(id, amount)`
           пересобирается без правок, но уже собранные сборки ссылаются на старую сигнатуру. Это критическое
           изменение на двоичном уровне: сервис или пакет, собранный с 1.0.0, получает `MissingMethodException` во
           время выполнения, когда в процесс попадает 1.1.0, например транзитивно через другой пакет.
         - `Deconstruct` получает третий параметр `out`: `var (orderId, amount) = message;` и позиционный шаблон из
           двух элементов перестают компилироваться (критическое изменение исходного кода), а уже собранный код снова
           получает `MissingMethodException`.
         - Новое свойство участвует в равенстве по значению: сообщения, которые раньше считались равными
           (дедупликация, ключи кэша), могут стать разными. Это изменение поведения.
      3. **Переименование, перестановка, удаление.** Переименование параметра удаляет свойство со старым именем,
         ломает именованные аргументы и, если тип сериализуется по именам свойств, формат на проводе. Перестановка
         параметров одного типа (`string From, string To`) опаснее всего: сигнатура не меняется, всё компилируется и
         запускается, а значения молча меняются местами. Удаление параметра ломает всё сразу.
      4. **Если позиционный контракт уже опубликован.** Совместимость можно сохранить вручную: явный конструктор со
         старой сигнатурой, который вызывает основной через `: this(orderId, amount, "EUR")`, и перегрузка
         `Deconstruct` со старым числом параметров. Цена: у типа становится два публичных конструктора с параметрами,
         и десериализацию через `System.Text.Json` надо перепроверить, потому что при нескольких таких конструкторах
         сериализатор требует явно указать нужный атрибутом `[JsonConstructor]`. Без этих заплаток изменение - мажорная
         версия пакета по SemVer.
      5. **Дизайн для долгой жизни.** Для общих контрактов выбирать номинальные записи:
         `public sealed record OrderPlaced { public required Guid OrderId { get; init; } public decimal Amount { get; init; } }`.
         Равенство по значению и `with` остаются, а новое необязательное свойство
         `public string? Currency { get; init; }` - это просто новый член: старые сборки работают, инициализаторы
         объектов компилируются. `required` ставить только на члены, которые есть с первой версии: новый обязательный
         член ломает компиляцию у всех, кто создаёт объект. `sealed` объявлять сразу: запечатать тип позже - критическое
         изменение, а иерархии позиционных записей распространяют любое изменение базовой записи на наследников у
         потребителей.
      6. **Процесс.** Проверка совместимости в CI: валидация пакетов в .NET SDK (`EnablePackageValidation` с базовой
         версией пакета) или анализатор публичного API. SemVer, где мажорная версия - единственное место для
         критических изменений. Удаление через `[Obsolete]` и период устаревания. Несовместимое по смыслу изменение -
         новый тип сообщения (`OrderPlacedV2`), который публикуется параллельно со старым.
      7. **Архитектурный уровень.** Общая сборка с типами связывает графики развёртывания всех сервисов. Для
         межсервисных сообщений надёжнее считать контрактом формат на проводе (JSON Schema, `.proto`) с правилами
         терпимого чтения (игнорировать неизвестные поля, иметь значения по умолчанию для отсутствующих), а пакет с
         типами держать тонким: без логики и с минимумом зависимостей.
    explanation: |
      Собранный IL ссылается на конструктор или метод по имени и полной сигнатуре с типами параметров, и CLR ищет
      ровно такой член. Значения параметров по умолчанию в C# - удобство компилятора в точке вызова, а не часть
      поиска метода, поэтому «необязательный» параметр совместим только на уровне исходного кода и только для вызовов
      конструктора. Руководство .NET по критическим изменениям различает изменения исходного кода, двоичные и
      поведенческие. Для общего пакета в парке сервисов двоичное изменение самое опасное: оно проявляется не при вашей
      сборке, а во время выполнения чужого процесса, после того как NuGet выбрал одну версию пакета на весь граф
      зависимостей, и сборка, скомпилированная с 1.0.0, работает рядом с 1.1.0.

      Позиционный синтаксис оптимизирован под краткость. Он хорош внутри одного сервиса или решения, где все вызовы
      пересобираются вместе, но в долгоживущем публичном API превращает порядок и состав параметров в контракт сразу
      нескольких членов. Номинальная запись многословнее, зато каждое свойство - отдельный член, и добавление члена
      остаётся совместимым изменением.

      Описанное поведение относится к C# 14 и .NET 10; записи появились в C# 9, модификатор `required` - в C# 11.

  en:
    title: What are the risks of positional records as shared contracts in NuGet packages, and how do you design them to evolve?
    prompt: |
      Positional records such as `OrderPlaced` live in a shared NuGet package `Shop.Contracts` and serve as messages
      and DTOs for dozens of services that will live with this package for years. The services and other packages
      are built and deployed independently.

      In version 1.1.0 the team wants to add a currency:
      `public record OrderPlaced(Guid OrderId, decimal Amount, string Currency = "EUR");`

      - What breaks for consumers such as `BillingHandler`, and in what form: at compile time or at run time?
      - Which other changes to positional parameters are dangerous?
      - How do you design such contracts so that they can evolve, and what do you put into the process?
    hint: "Which public members does the compiler generate from one positional parameter, and how does the CLR find a constructor that an already compiled assembly calls?"
    answer: |
      1. **What becomes public API.** The compiler turns every positional parameter into several public members at
         once: a parameter of the primary constructor, an `init` property with the same name, an `out` parameter of
         the synthesized `Deconstruct` method (which positional patterns such as `OrderPlaced(_, > 1000m)` also use)
         and a part of `Equals`, `GetHashCode` and `ToString`. The order and types of the parameters become part of
         the signatures.
      2. **Adding a parameter, even with a default value.**
         - The constructor `OrderPlaced(Guid, decimal)` disappears and `OrderPlaced(Guid, decimal, string)` replaces it.
           The compiler inserts the default value at the call site, so `new OrderPlaced(id, amount)` rebuilds without
           edits, but assemblies that are already built reference the old signature. This is a binary breaking change:
           a service or package built against 1.0.0 gets `MissingMethodException` at run time when 1.1.0 ends up in
           the process, for example transitively through another package.
         - `Deconstruct` gets a third `out` parameter: `var (orderId, amount) = message;` and a positional pattern with
           two elements stop compiling (a source breaking change), and already built code again gets
           `MissingMethodException`.
         - The new property takes part in value equality: messages that used to be equal (deduplication, cache keys)
           can become different. This is a behavioral change.
      3. **Renaming, reordering, removing.** Renaming a parameter removes the property with the old name, breaks
         named arguments and, if the type is serialized by property names, the wire format. Reordering parameters of
         the same type (`string From, string To`) is the most dangerous: the signature does not change, everything
         compiles and runs, and the values are silently swapped. Removing a parameter breaks everything at once.
      4. **If a positional contract is already published.** You can keep compatibility by hand: an explicit
         constructor with the old signature that calls the primary one through `: this(orderId, amount, "EUR")`, and a
         `Deconstruct` overload with the old number of parameters. The cost: the type now has two public
         parameterized constructors, so deserialization with `System.Text.Json` must be rechecked, because with several
         such constructors the serializer requires the intended one to be marked with `[JsonConstructor]`. Without
         these patches the change is a major package version under SemVer.
      5. **Design for a long life.** For shared contracts choose nominal records:
         `public sealed record OrderPlaced { public required Guid OrderId { get; init; } public decimal Amount { get; init; } }`.
         Value equality and `with` stay, and a new optional property `public string? Currency { get; init; }` is just
         a new member: old assemblies keep working and object initializers compile. Put `required` only on members
         that exist from the first version: a new required member breaks compilation for everyone who creates the
         object. Declare `sealed` from the start: sealing a type later is a breaking change, and hierarchies of
         positional records spread any change of the base record to the derived records of consumers.
      6. **Process.** A compatibility check in CI: package validation in the .NET SDK (`EnablePackageValidation` with a
         baseline package version) or a public API analyzer. SemVer, where the major version is the only place for
         breaking changes. Removal through `[Obsolete]` and a deprecation period. A change that is incompatible in
         meaning becomes a new message type (`OrderPlacedV2`) published side by side with the old one.
      7. **Architecture level.** A shared assembly of types couples the deployment schedules of all services. For
         messages between services it is more robust to treat the wire format (JSON Schema, `.proto`) as the contract,
         with tolerant reader rules (ignore unknown fields, have defaults for missing ones), and to keep the types
         package thin: no logic and a minimum of dependencies.
    explanation: |
      Compiled IL references a constructor or method by name and full signature including parameter types, and the
      CLR looks for exactly that member. Default parameter values in C# are a compiler convenience at the call site,
      not part of member lookup, so an "optional" parameter is compatible only at the source level and only for
      constructor calls. The .NET guidance on breaking changes distinguishes source, binary and behavioral changes.
      For a shared package in a fleet of services a binary change is the most dangerous: it shows up not in your
      build but at run time in someone else's process, after NuGet has picked one package version for the whole
      dependency graph and an assembly compiled against 1.0.0 runs next to 1.1.0.

      The positional syntax is optimized for brevity. It works well inside one service or solution, where all call
      sites are rebuilt together, but in a long-lived public API it turns the order and set of parameters into the
      contract of several members at once. A nominal record is more verbose, but every property is a separate member,
      and adding a member stays a compatible change.

      The behaviour described applies to C# 14 and .NET 10; records arrived in C# 9 and the `required` modifier in C# 11.

      - "Records (C# reference)"

      - "Package validation overview"

    title: Does changing a return type from string to string? in a shared NuGet package break consumers?
    prompt: |
      An internal NuGet package compiled with `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` is used by about 40 services. It has the
      method `public string GetDisplayName(int userId)`. In the next version the author changes the declaration to
      `public string? GetDisplayName(int userId)`, because the user may be missing, and in that case the method now
      returns `null`. Some of the services build with `<TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>`.

      Which statement about this change is true?
    hint: Does the IL signature of the method differ for `string` and `string?`? And who reads the `?` annotation - the CLR when the method is called, or the compiler when the consumer is built?
    options:
      a: "It is a binary breaking change: the return type in the method signature changes, so services compiled against the previous version of the package get `MissingMethodException` until they are rebuilt."
      b: "It is binary compatible: in IL both versions return `System.String`, and the annotation is stored in an attribute that only the compiler reads. But services that rebuild with a nullable context enabled get warnings such as CS8602, and a build with warnings as errors fails, so it is a contract change."
      c: "It is not a breaking change at all: the annotation is only a hint, it affects neither the build nor the execution of consumers, so it can ship in a patch release without notice."
      d: "Only services with `<Nullable>disable</Nullable>` are affected: their build fails because they cannot handle a `string?` return type, while services with nullable enabled already expect `null` from any reference type."
    optionExplanations:
      a: "The `?` on a reference type does not change the type in the signature: in IL the method still returns `System.String`, and the annotation is written into the `NullableAttribute` and `NullableContextAttribute` attributes. At run time the method is bound by its signature, so services that are already compiled find it and keep working without a rebuild."
      c: "The annotation is part of the contract that the consumer's compiler reads. After a rebuild, code that accesses members of the result or assigns it to a `string` variable gets warnings, and with warnings as errors the build fails. More importantly, the method really returns `null` now, and already compiled code without a check will get `NullReferenceException` at run time. Shipping it quietly in a patch release hides this contract change."
      d: "It is the other way round. In a disabled nullable context the compiler reports no nullable warnings at all, so such services build as before (though they may get `NullReferenceException` at run time). The warnings appear precisely in services with nullable enabled: there `string` means \"never `null`\", and the compiler tracks the flow of a `string?` value."
    answer: "The change is binary compatible because the annotation is metadata used only by the compiler, but on rebuild consumers with nullable enabled get warnings, and a build with warnings as errors fails."
    explanation: |
      Nullable reference types introduce no new types in the CLR. `string` and `string?` in a method signature are
      the same `System.String`, and the difference is recorded in assembly attributes read by the compiler that
      builds the consumer. So an annotation change has to be judged against the different kinds of compatibility
      that the Microsoft .NET library guidance distinguishes:

      - **Binary compatibility is kept.** The signature did not change, so services compiled against the previous
        version load the package and call the method without a rebuild.
      - **Source compatibility breaks for some consumers.** When rebuilt with a nullable context enabled, the
        expression `name.Length` produces CS8602 (dereference of a possibly null reference), and
        `string name = GetDisplayName(id);` produces CS8600. In a normal build these are warnings, but with
        `TreatWarningsAsErrors` the build fails, and a package update blocks teams that did not plan for it.
      - **Behaviour changes.** The annotation was changed because the method started returning `null`. That is the
        real contract change: consumers that are not rebuilt, or build without a nullable context, get no warnings
        at all and find out through `NullReferenceException` in production.

      For an architect this means an annotation change in a shared package must be versioned and announced as a
      contract change, not treated as cosmetics. It is often safer not to change the semantics of the existing
      method but to add another one, for example `TryGetDisplayName` or `FindDisplayName` returning `string?`, keep
      the old one with its "never `null`" guarantee and mark it `[Obsolete]`. Relaxing a parameter (`string` to
      `string?`) and strengthening a return guarantee (`string?` to `string`) are usually safe for callers; the
      opposite changes produce warnings.

      This is how it works since C# 8, including on .NET 10.

      - "Nullable reference types"

    using System.Runtime.CompilerServices;
    using System.Runtime.ExceptionServices;

    class Program
    {
        static void Main()
        {
            try
            {
                Rethrow();
            }
            catch (Exception ex)
            {
                Console.Write(ex.StackTrace.Contains("ThrowOriginal"));
            }
        }

        static void Rethrow()
        {
            ExceptionDispatchInfo captured = null;
            try
            {
                ThrowOriginal();
            }
            catch (InvalidOperationException ex)
            {
                captured = ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture(ex);
            }

            // Thrown later, outside the catch block
            captured.Throw();
        }

    hint: Что именно запоминает `ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture`, кроме ссылки на сам объект исключения?
    options:
      a: "True"
      b: "False"
      c: Необработанное исключение `InvalidOperationException`
      d: Ошибка компиляции
    optionExplanations:
      b: "`False` получилось бы при `throw ex;`: такой выброс начинает трассировку заново с точки повторного выброса. `ExceptionDispatchInfo.Throw` восстанавливает сохранённую трассировку, поэтому кадр `ThrowOriginal` в ней остаётся."
      c: "`captured.Throw()` действительно выбрасывает `InvalidOperationException`, но вызов `Rethrow()` в `Main` обёрнут в `try` с `catch (Exception ex)`, поэтому исключение перехвачено и программа завершается нормально."

    answer: "True"
    explanation: |
      `ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture(ex)` сохраняет не только ссылку на исключение, но и состояние его трассировки
      стека на момент захвата. Метод `Throw` выбрасывает тот же объект исключения, восстанавливает сохранённую

      исходного выброса (`ThrowOriginal`), затем строка-разделитель вида `--- End of stack trace from previous
      location ---`, затем кадры `Rethrow` и `Main`. Поэтому `Contains("ThrowOriginal")` возвращает `True`.

      Сравните с альтернативами:

      - `throw;` сохраняет трассировку, но допустим только внутри блока `catch`.
      - `throw ex;` можно написать где угодно, но трассировка начнётся заново с места этого оператора, и кадр

      теряя причину сбоя. Тот же механизм использует `await`: исключение из задачи выбрасывается в продолжении с

      примера: он не даёт JIT встроить метод и убрать его кадр из трассировки. Результат проверен для .NET 10.

    prompt: |
      The `Rethrow` method catches an exception, saves it with `ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture` and throws it again
      after leaving the `catch` block. The caller checks whether `StackTrace` contains the method that originally
      threw the exception. What does this program print in .NET 10?
    hint: What exactly does `ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture` remember besides the reference to the exception object?

      a: "True"
      b: "False"
      c: Unhandled `InvalidOperationException`
      d: Compile error
    optionExplanations:
      b: "`False` is what `throw ex;` would give: that statement starts the stack trace again from the rethrow point. `ExceptionDispatchInfo.Throw` restores the captured trace, so the `ThrowOriginal` frame stays in it."
      c: "`captured.Throw()` does throw `InvalidOperationException`, but the call to `Rethrow()` in `Main` is wrapped in a `try` with `catch (Exception ex)`, so the exception is caught and the program ends normally."
      d: "The code is valid: `ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture` and the instance method `Throw` exist in `System.Runtime.ExceptionServices`, and assigning `null` to a local variable is allowed."
    answer: "True"
    explanation: |
      `ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture(ex)` stores not only a reference to the exception but also the state of its
      stack trace at the moment of capture. The `Throw` method throws the same exception object, restores the
      captured trace and appends the frames from the rethrow point. The final `StackTrace` first lists the frames of
      the original throw (`ThrowOriginal`), then a separator line such as `--- End of stack trace from previous
      location ---`, then the frames of `Rethrow` and `Main`. That is why `Contains("ThrowOriginal")` returns `True`.

      Compare the alternatives:

      - `throw;` keeps the stack trace, but it is allowed only inside a `catch` block.
      - `throw ex;` can be written anywhere, but the trace starts again at that statement and the `ThrowOriginal`
        frame is lost: the output would be `False`.

      `ExceptionDispatchInfo` exists for exactly the case where an exception must be thrown later or somewhere
      else without losing the cause of the failure. `await` uses the same mechanism: an exception from a task is
      thrown in the continuation with its original stack trace.

      The `MethodImpl(MethodImplOptions.NoInlining)` attribute on `ThrowOriginal` only keeps the example stable: it
      stops the JIT from inlining the method and removing its frame from the trace. The result was checked for .NET 10.

      - "ExceptionDispatchInfo class"
      - "Best practices for exceptions"

      `FirstChanceException` is raised when an exception is thrown in managed code, before the runtime starts
      searching the call stack for a handler. At that moment nobody knows yet whether the exception will be
      caught, so the event fires for all exceptions: those that will end up unhandled and those that a `catch`
      in your code, in a library or in the framework will catch right away.

      This has practical consequences for the "log everything" idea:

      - **Noise.** The log gets exceptions that code expects and handles itself, for example
        `OperationCanceledException` when a request is cancelled. A first-chance log is a useful diagnostic
        signal, but it does not replace logging in `catch` blocks and handling `AppDomain.UnhandledException`.
      - **Cost.** The handler runs on every throw, so heavy logging slows down exceptions, which are already
        expensive, on a hot path.
      - **Observation only.** The event arguments give access to the exception object, but they do not let you
        mark it handled or change the subsequent search for a `catch`.

        event is raised recursively and can end in a stack overflow. This includes exceptions that the logger
        throws and catches internally, which is why the handler is usually protected with a per-thread
        re-entrancy flag and a `try`/`catch` around the write.

  en:
    title: "Should business failures move from exceptions to a Result type, and how do you set the team policy?"
    prompt: |
      Half of the team wants to move all business failures (validation, "not found", insufficient funds, version
      conflicts) from exceptions to a `Result<T>` return type, the other half is against it. The service already
      runs in production, and the code mixes both approaches. How do you make the decision, where do you draw the
      line between an exception and a result, and how do you roll the policy out in the team?
    hint: |
      For each kind of failure, ask who is supposed to react to it and how often it happens in normal operation.
    answer: |
      **Decision**

      1. **Start with data, not with the argument.** Collect which exceptions the service throws and where they are
         caught. An exception caught in the same or a neighbouring method and turned into a response is control
         flow through exceptions. Check the frequency in the runtime metrics: an exception on every tenth request
         and an exception once a week are different cases.
      2. **Draw the line by the method contract.** The criterion: is the immediate caller expected to handle this
         outcome and choose a branch?
         - Yes (validation, "not found", insufficient funds, a business conflict): it is a legitimate result of the
           operation and becomes part of the signature, a `Result<T>` with a closed set of typed errors or the
           `Try...` pattern.
         - No (a broken invariant, `null` where it cannot be, an unavailable database, a timeout): an exception.
           The caller can do nothing sensible with it, so it travels to the application boundary or to a retry
           policy.
      3. **Apply it per layer, consistently.** The domain and application layers return results for business
         outcomes. Infrastructure throws exceptions and does not wrap them into `Result`. The boundary (a controller,
         a message handler) maps result errors to specific responses (400, 404, 409) and exceptions to 500 through
         the central handler. The same outcome must not be an exception in one module and a result in another.
      4. **What not to do.** Do not return an `Exception` object as a value: the .NET design guidelines forbid it
         explicitly. Do not write `catch (Exception ex)` that converts into `Result.Fail(ex.Message)`: the stack
         trace is lost, and programming errors are disguised as business outcomes. Do not create members that throw
         or not depending on a flag.
      5. **One type for the whole team.** One `Result` (your own or from one chosen library), with errors as typed
         codes or records, not strings. C# 14 (.NET 10) has no built-in discriminated unions, and the compiler does
         not force the caller to inspect a returned value, so without conventions and code review a result is easy
         to ignore.

      **Rollout**

      - An ADR: the criterion, an "exception or result" table for typical cases, the mapping template at the
        boundary.
      - New code and one pilot module follow the rule from day one; old code is converted when it is changed
        anyway. No mass rewrite.
      - Public APIs of shared libraries are not changed silently: replacing an exception with a result breaks
        consumers. That is a separate decision, a new version or a new method alongside, following the `Parse`
        and `TryParse` pair.
      - A code review checklist item: "is this an expected outcome, and who handles it?".
      - After a few iterations check: are there fewer exceptions per request, are handlers easier to read, have
        ignored results appeared? Adjust the ADR accordingly.
    explanation: |
      Both halves of the team are partly right. The .NET design guidelines recommend reporting failures with
      exceptions rather than error codes: an error code can go unchecked and the failure goes unnoticed, while an
      exception carries a stack trace and stops execution. But the same guidelines ask you to avoid exceptions for
      normal control flow and to consider their cost: throwing is expensive, and the method signature does not
      show which business outcomes the caller should expect.

      The contradiction disappears with the definition of a failure. The guidelines call it a failure when a member
      cannot do what it was designed to do. If "order not found" is a legitimate answer of a lookup method, it is
      not a failure but a result, just like `false` from `TryParse`. So the decision is made about the contract of
      each method, not about coding style in general.

      Both extremes are equally bad. `Result` for everything turns infrastructure failures into values that must
      be passed by hand through every layer, loses the stack trace, and a forgotten check silently swallows an
      error - exactly the error-code problem the guidelines warn about. Exceptions for everything hide business
      logic in `catch` blocks and add cost on hot paths.

      For a lead the key points are consistency and gradual change. Mixed rules are worse than either pure
      approach, and a mass rewrite is risky and gives users nothing. The policy is set per layer with one
      criterion, written into an ADR and checked in code review. The statements about syntax refer to C# 14 and
      .NET 10.
    linkTitles:
      - "Best practices for exceptions"
      - "Design guidelines: exception throwing"

    title: Какое изменение исключений публичного метода библиотеки не ломает совместимость в минорной версии?

    options:

    title: Which change to the exceptions of a public library method does not break compatibility in a minor version?
    prompt: |
      Your team ships a shared NuGet library that other teams use. The documentation of its public methods lists

      c: "After `Dispose`, throw `InvalidOperationException` instead of the documented `ObjectDisposedException`."

  en:
    title: Why do production stack traces have no line numbers, and how should you set up build and release so they do?
    prompt: |
      Your team owns a .NET 10 service. In production logs, exception stack traces contain method names but no
      file names and no line numbers. Dumps taken during past incidents cannot be matched to the source code of
      the version that was running at the time.

      Select all build and release practices that fix this and keep dumps debuggable later.
    hint: Where is the mapping from IL code to source lines stored, and what happens to that file on its way from the build to production and to whoever analyzes the dump?
    options:
      a: "Check that the `.pdb` files from the publish output actually reach the server or the container image: a Dockerfile or pipeline step that copies only `*.dll` files, or `DebugType` set to `none`, leaves the runtime without symbols."
      b: "Deploy the Debug configuration to production, because the Release configuration removes line information from the assembly."
      c: "Set `<DebugType>embedded</DebugType>`: the portable PDB is stored inside the assembly itself, so it cannot be lost or mismatched separately from the DLL."
      d: "Log `ex.ToString()` instead of `ex.Message`: file names and line numbers are then read from the IL metadata of the assembly, and no PDB is needed."
      e: "Archive the PDBs of every release build (a symbol server or build artifacts with a retention policy) and enable Source Link, so a dump taken months later opens with matching symbols and the sources of the exact commit."
      f: "Rely on Source Link alone and strip PDBs from the image: Source Link writes repository URLs into the assembly, and the runtime uses them to restore line numbers in stack traces."
    optionExplanations:
      b: "In SDK-style projects the Release configuration also produces a portable PDB with line information by default. Release differs by having optimizations on, not by lacking symbols. Debug in production hurts performance and does not help if the PDB still never reaches the server."
      d: "`ToString()` does add the stack trace, but IL metadata has no file names or line numbers: they exist only in the PDB. Without symbols the trace still has no lines."
      f: "Source Link stores the mapping from file paths to repository URLs inside the PDB. Without the PDB there are neither line numbers nor Source Link data. Besides, Source Link is for a debugger downloading sources, not for the runtime building a stack trace."
    answer: "Check that the `.pdb` files reach production; embed the PDB in the assembly with `DebugType` `embedded`; archive the symbols of every release and enable Source Link."
    explanation: |
      Line numbers and file names are not stored in the assembly's IL. The compiler writes them to a symbol file
      (PDB), which maps IL offsets to source lines. When the runtime builds a `StackTrace`, it looks for a
      portable PDB next to the assembly (a file with the same name and the `.pdb` extension) or inside the
      assembly itself if the PDB is embedded. The PDB must match exactly this assembly: an identifier in the
      assembly and in the PDB is compared, and symbols from a different build do not fit. No matching PDB means
      the trace keeps only method names.

      That leads to three practices:

      - **The PDB reaches production.** The usual cause of loss is not the compiler but delivery: a Dockerfile
        copies only `*.dll`, a pipeline deletes `*.pdb` "to save space", or someone set `DebugType` to `none`.
        CI can check for this.
      - **The PDB is embedded in the assembly.** With `DebugType` `embedded` there is no separate `.pdb` file,
        the symbols travel with the DLL and cannot be lost on the way. The cost is a somewhat larger assembly.
      - **Symbols are archived and Source Link is on.** A dump is analyzed later and on another machine, so the
        PDBs of every release are kept on a symbol server or in build artifacts for at least the support window
        of that version. Source Link records in the PDB where the sources of the specific commit live in the
        repository, and the debugger downloads the right files itself. The documentation also recommends setting
        `ContinuousIntegrationBuild` in CI so that the paths in the PDB are deterministic.

      For a lead this is above all a process decision: symbols are part of the release artifact, their presence
      is checked automatically, and keeping symbols is part of the release retention policy. The behaviour is
      described for .NET 10.
    linkTitles:
      - "C# compiler options: code generation (DebugType, Optimize)"
      - "Source Link in .NET libraries"
      - "Symbols in .NET diagnostics"

  en:
    title: How do you design crash dump collection and analysis for hundreds of .NET service instances?
    prompt: |
      Your company runs several hundred instances of .NET 10 services in several Kubernetes clusters, owned by
      dozens of teams. Today crashes are investigated by luck: the container restarts, the dump, if there was one,
      is lost with it, and nobody can tell whether a crash is new or the same one seen a month ago.

      Design crash dump collection and analysis for the whole fleet so that it still works several years from
      now. What is configured on the instances, where do dumps go, who can read them, and how does a dump turn
      into a ticket for the right team?
    hint: |
      Follow the path of one dump: where it is written at the moment of the crash, what you need to read it a year
      later, and how you tell 500 dumps of one bug from 500 different bugs.
    answer: |
      1. **Collection is a platform default, not a team choice.** The base image or the deployment template sets
         the runtime variables on every instance: `DOTNET_DbgEnableMiniDump=1`, the dump type in
         `DOTNET_DbgMiniDumpType`, `DOTNET_DbgMiniDumpName` with placeholders such as `%e` (executable name),
         `%p` (PID), `%h` (host) and `%t` (time) pointing to a dedicated volume, and `DOTNET_EnableCrashReport=1`
         for a JSON crash report next to the dump. The dump type is a fleet decision: heap (type 2, the default)
         for most services, full only where native memory matters, and the size budget follows from that choice.
         The container memory limit and the volume size leave headroom for writing the dump, otherwise the dump
         itself gets the container killed or fills the node disk.
      2. **Know what this does not cover.** A process killed from the outside (an OOM kill, `SIGKILL` after the
         grace period) gets no chance to write a dump. Those cases are covered by metrics and by triggered dumps
         taken from a live process (for example `dotnet-monitor` collection rules on memory or CPU), which then
         go through the same pipeline.
      3. **Ship it and do not keep it locally.** An agent on the node or a sidecar uploads every new dump and
         crash report to central storage, attaches metadata (service, version, commit, image digest, runtime
         version, cluster, pod, time) and deletes the local file. It rate-limits: a pod in a crash loop must not
         send a thousand identical dumps; after the first few dumps per signature and version, crash reports are
         enough.
      4. **Treat dumps as sensitive data.** Heap and full dumps contain tokens, connection strings and personal
         data. The storage is separate, encrypted and in the required region; read access is granted to the
         owning team on request, for a limited time and with an audit trail; retention is short for dumps (for
         example weeks) and longer for crash reports and signatures; deletion is automatic. Most people work with
         the extracted stacks, not with the dump itself.
      5. **Archive the symbols of every build.** CI publishes the PDBs of every released build to a symbol server
         or an artifact store keyed by build, together with Source Link, so stack frames point to the exact
         commit. Runtime symbols and the DAC are downloaded from the Microsoft symbol server with `dotnet-symbol`;
         for self-contained apps or custom runtime builds the team archives them itself. Symbols are kept at least
         as long as any dump or supported version that needs them.
      6. **Automated triage by stack signature.** A worker opens each new dump (a scripted `dotnet-dump analyze`
         or a ClrMD-based tool) or reads the crash report, takes the exception type and the top frames of the
         faulting thread, normalizes them (no offsets, addresses or lambda numbers) and hashes them into a
         signature. Crashes are grouped by signature and counted per version and cluster, and a new signature
         after a deployment opens a ticket for the owning team with links to the dumps.
      7. **Keep it working for years.** The platform team owns the pipeline; the configuration is checked on every
         runtime upgrade (variable names, dump types, analysis tool versions); a synthetic crash in a staging
         environment on every platform release proves the whole chain end to end, from the crash to the ticket.
    explanation: |
      At fleet scale the hard part is not taking a dump but everything around it. A dump nobody can read is
      worthless: without the exact PDBs of that build and the matching runtime binaries, the analyst sees
      addresses instead of methods, and a year later the build agent that had them is gone. A dump nobody finds is
      worthless too: if it stays on the node, it disappears with the container. That is why collection is switched
      on by the template, and shipping, symbols and triage are parts of one pipeline.

      Grouping by signature turns a stream of files into a short list of bugs. Hundreds of instances of one
      service crash on the same bug at the same time; without grouping every crash looks like a separate incident,
      and with it the team sees "signature X, 400 crashes, started with version 2.3.1". It is the normalization of
      the frames that keeps the signature stable between builds.

      Size, privacy and cost pull in the same direction: collect a rich dump rarely, keep it briefly and restrict
      access to it; keep cheap artifacts (crash reports, signatures, counts) for a long time and share them widely.
      A good design names these trade-offs explicitly: dump type, sampling per signature, retention and who may
      read.

      The configuration described here is for .NET 10 on Linux, and the variables use the `DOTNET_` prefix. Re-check
      the variable names and supported placeholders on every runtime upgrade.
    linkTitles:
      - "Collect dumps on crash"
      - "Symbols and PDBs in .NET"
      - "dotnet-symbol utility: downloading symbols for dumps"

      only at run time.

        is guaranteed (for example, `List<T>`);

      One restriction remained: an interface cannot hold instance state. It cannot declare an instance field, an

      static members.

      abstract class. An interface describes behaviour, not the data of an object. The answer holds for C# 14 and
